A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Prescribe-then-Select framework and two optimization tasks. Text, equations, figures, tables, and all appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison, including v2's new Appendices E and F.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments on multi-product newsvendor and shipment planning, including segment-wise performance, policy comparisons, and learned-tree examples.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments, evaluates an additional neural-network policy, and reports new runtime and memory results.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1.2 and 5.3 add the neural-network point-prediction policy PPt-NN to PS's candidate library, expanding it from five policies to six. Cross-validated cost construction, OPT ensemble training, policy refitting, and majority-vote selection remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four-product newsvendor and four-facility/four-location shipment-planning tasks with the same three synthetic demand segments per task. The additional policy and runtime measurements do not expand dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: PPt-NN is added to the segment-wise and aggregate comparisons in v2's Figures 1, 4, and 5. The original SAA, PP-kNN, PPt-kNN, PP-RF, and PPt-RF comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a neural-network configuration with hidden layers (16, 32, 16), ReLU, and early stopping, plus stage-wise runtime evaluation. Appendix B corrects the stated weekday domain from [6] to {0,...,6}, without establishing that data generation was rerun. The main training-size schedule and held-out evaluation design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix E analyzes computational bottlenecks and selector overhead through component-wise timings across training sizes and a peak-memory report. The existing segment analyses, convergence analysis, and illustrative trees are retained; Appendix D's added explanation does not introduce new tree examples.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 100 independent training samples per size and two-sided 95% Student-t confidence intervals for performance. Appendix E newly reports runtime averages over 10 randomly sampled training datasets, without runtime confidence intervals or an increase in the original performance-run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds PPt-NN performance results and updates comparisons involving the expanded PS library. Section 5.4.2 changes the shipment finding at N = 3000 from disjoint to slightly overlapping confidence intervals. New Tables 4–5 report runtimes, including 1064.69 seconds for newsvendor optimization versus 31.21 seconds for the meta-policy at N = 5000.

T1.justification: Appendix F explicitly formulates the regularized empirical tree objective, including split penalty and depth/leaf-size constraints, and derives the leafwise optimal policy assignment in Equations 6–7. These add mathematical specificity to the existing training description; Lemma 1 and its proof remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: feasible contextual policy selection, improvements under heterogeneous policy performance, and convergence to a dominant policy. The added evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds a finite-sample rationale despite some base policies' asymptotic optimality. Its computational discussion shifts from emphasizing additional cross-validation cost to modest selector overhead relative to evaluating multiple policies. The conclusion also acknowledges settings where policy averaging is feasible.

D1.justification: v2 supplies neural-network hyperparameters, explicit OPT optimization details, and clarification that shipment evaluation solves recourse using realized demand. It adds runtime and memory information and replaces the anonymous code-access link with a named GitHub repository link. These disclosures do not establish changes to the retained procedures.

R1.justification: v2 adds six references, including Hu et al. (2022) and Zhou et al. (2023), supporting discussion of regret rates, data generation, and neural networks. It qualifies the criticism of policy averaging and more explicitly positions OPT's treatments as entire constrained optimization pipelines.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized explanatory and grammatical revisions, corrects terminology such as 'Predict-then-Select,' and adds publication information. Sections 1–6 and Appendices A–D retain their organization, with new runtime and OPT explanations appended as E and F.

P2.justification: The newsvendor segment plot moves from Figure 3 in the results to Figure 1 in the problem setting. Performance plots gain NN curves and adjusted legends/axes, pipeline graphics and captions are revised, and two runtime tables are added. Tables 1–3 and the illustrative tree graphics are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the study with an evaluated NN candidate, measured computational costs, and clearer OPT training and feasibility-evaluation details. These improve auditability without changing the central experimental scope. The gains are limited: runtime measurements combine selector training and inference, so they do not separately substantiate the new negligible-inference-latency claim.
